clue.text: Sign programme's finishing early

indicators.note: the title stops one letter before its proper end, so its last letter goes

parts.note: The Archers is the long-running BBC radio soap opera about a farming village

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a broadcast show is ending before its scheduled time.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archers is a BBC radio soap; 'finishing early' cuts its final S. 'Sign' looks like a notice but is a zodiac sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Sagittarius, one of the twelve zodiac signs, is represented as a bowman, so it is known by this title.

clue.text: See 26
Leaving? Rousing cheer initially let out

indicators.note: the letter is released from the longer word, so it is removed

parts.note: rousing means exciting

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word cheer is wanted here

explanation.surface: A departing person is given a stirring send-off, with a cheer started and then released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes C from 'cheer', and 'let out' removes that C from EXCITING.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is leaving a room is in the act of going out of it, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: No money for accommodation on square? Spend the night here

indicators.note: in a down answer, placing one piece on another sets it after it
says the money is absent, so that letter is removed from the word

parts.note: rooms are accommodation, as in rooms to let
T stands for a square, as in the draughtsman's T-square tool

explanation.surface: A traveller with no cash looks for somewhere to sleep near a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove M from ROOMS to leave ROOS, then add T, a loose crossword use for square from the T-square.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is the perch where birds settle to sleep, so it is a place where one spends the night.

clue.text: See 9
Cardinal's displeasure at court summons originally is diverting

parts.note: cardinals wear red, so red is the cardinal colour
ire is anger or displeasure

indicators.note: the word's first letter only is taken, as from its origin

explanation.surface: A senior churchman's anger at being called to court is somehow amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diverting' looks like 'amusing' in the surface, but here it means sending another way.
explanation.definitionFit: To redirect something is to send it on a different route, just as diverting traffic or post does.

clue.text: Look, fellows, current's coming in!

indicators.note: the current enters the word for fellows, sitting inside it

parts.note: fellows are men
I is the symbol for electric current in physics

explanation.surface: Someone shouts to a group of men to look at the tide or stream arriving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look' sounds like a command but is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's mien is their appearance or bearing, the way they look to others.

clue.text: Undertaking counterpart of 8, might one say, that's timeless?

indicators.note: time is abbreviated T, so being without time means that letter is dropped

parts.note: the answer to 8 is HIT IT OFF; swapping each part for its opposite gives miss it on, a playful invented opposite

explanation.surface: A question about whether an undertaking that mirrors another one could last forever.
explanation.walkthrough: HIT becomes MISS and OFF becomes ON, giving MISS IT ON; dropping its T leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mission is a task or assignment someone takes on, which is an undertaking.

clue.text: Skin deep wound — one kept getting careless taking E's

indicators.note: joins the two pieces, the first gaining the second
the scrambled letters hold the one inside them
wound as in twisted round, so the letters of deep are wound into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: taking away, so the named letters E and S leave the word

parts.note: remiss means careless or negligent

explanation.surface: A deep cut on a careless drug-taker who keeps taking ecstasy pills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skin deep' reads as one phrase, but 'Skin' alone is the definition. In 'taking E's', taking means taking away, and the E's are the letters E and S, not ecstasy tablets.
explanation.definitionFit: The epidermis is the outermost layer of the skin in anatomy.

clue.text: Get on well with one posh bloke after bonk

indicators.note: the pieces for one and the posh bloke come after the hit

parts.note: to bonk is to hit, as with a blow to the head
I is the Roman numeral for one
a toff is an upper-class man in British slang

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about getting along with an upper-class man after a romp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bonk' suggests sex in British slang, but here it is a blow. A toff is a posh person in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: To hit it off is an idiom for forming an instant friendly rapport with someone.

clue.text: A lot of cleaning staff to keep home going for actor

indicators.note: most but not all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: dusting is a form of cleaning
H is an abbreviation for home, as in sports results
off means going, as in I'm off
to staff is to man, as in manning a desk

explanation.surface: Plenty of cleaners hired to look after a house while its owner is away, for some actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' means most of the word, so only its last letter is cut. H for home is a sports-results convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Dustin Hoffman is the American film star of The Graduate and Rain Man.

clue.text: Will one want people getting on with the job?

definitions.text: Will one want people getting on with the job?

parts.words: Will one want people getting on with the job?
parts.note: people getting on are elderly people; a person prejudiced by age would not want older workers in a post

explanation.walkthrough: 'getting on with the job' reads as working diligently, but 'getting on' means growing old.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone discriminating on grounds of age would not want older employees kept in their posts.

clue.text: Enforcer-in-chief's right — extremist spilling his guts

indicators.note: the right sits in the word for chief

parts.note: main means chief, as in the main reason; the 's reads as is

indicators.note: the extremist loses his inside letters, keeping only the first and last

explanation.surface: An extremist confesses everything and the man in charge is proved correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enforcer-in-chief' looks like one hyphenated title, but 'in' is the containment signal: read 'in chief's right' as 'right is in chief'.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a strict disciplinarian who insists on rules being obeyed, named after a French drillmaster.

clue.text: It could be an Oxford way of speaking

definitions.meaning: an Oxford is a style of lace-up shoe, and a ... is a decorated shoe that can be made in that style
a strong regional accent, especially Irish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford way of speaking' suggests a posh university accent; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a sturdy perforated shoe and a pronounced regional accent.

clue.text: No reason to be worried about end of term feature

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go round that letter
worried letters are fretted and twisted into a new order
the final letter of the word term

explanation.surface: A teacher reassures someone there's no need for anxiety about the close of the school term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts the scrambled NO REASON around M, the last letter of 'term'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman nose is a prominent nose with a high bridge, a facial feature.

clue.text: Tell blonde nurses to come around

indicators.note: the nurses gather round the blonde, one on each side

parts.note: EN is an enrolled nurse; two of them, one EN after another, for the plural
light hair is blonde

explanation.surface: An instruction to tell a fair-haired patient that the nurses will come round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell' sounds like 'order' but is the definition; two ENs flank LIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlighten someone is to inform them, giving them knowledge they lacked.

clue.text: Can mean trouble, as Billy the Kid was

parts.note: the can and the nick are both slang for prison

indicators.note: to trouble is to disturb, so the letters of mean are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: Prison could mean trouble, as it did for the outlaw Billy the Kid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the verb but is slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Billy the Kid was the alias of the outlaw Henry McCarty, a name others called him by.

clue.text: Small vessels in which one crosses over river

parts.note: A is the indefinite article, meaning one

indicators.note: the crosses lie over the river, covering it

parts.note: mules are crosses between a horse and a donkey
the Po is the main river of northern Italy

explanation.surface: Little boats in which a person crosses a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crosses' looks like a verb but is a noun: mules are hybrids of horse and donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Ampoules are small sealed glass phials holding a dose of medicine, so they are little containers.

clue.text: Row about home getting low rating

indicators.note: the oar goes round the home

parts.note: an oar is used to row
a nest is a bird's home

explanation.surface: An argument about one's house earns a poor review.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with 'now' in the surface's quarrel, but here it is the boating sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A single star out of five is a poor review score for a hotel, film or product.

clue.text: Climax during drink! What did you say?

indicators.note: the climax happens inside the drinking

parts.note: to sup is to drink
a peak is a climax or high point

explanation.surface: Reaching a high point while drinking, then a puzzled query.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark belongs to the definition: it is what a listener says when they could not hear.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking someone to speak up is a request for them to talk louder because you could not hear them.

clue.text: Mate, I nearly forgot to back more than one English runner

indicators.note: the letters run backwards

parts.note: PS, a postscript, is what you add when you nearly forgot to say something
several English rivers are called the Ouse, and a river is a runner

explanation.surface: A punter almost forgot to bet on several English racehorses, telling a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runner' suggests a racehorse but is a river: there are several Ouses in England. PS reversed gives SP.
explanation.definitionFit: A mate is a partner in marriage, as in the phrase one's husband or wife.

clue.text: Having sustained success, Ronaldo left for Germany, surprisingly

indicators.note: the letters come out in an unexpected order
the letter for left stands in place of the one for Germany

parts.note: D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: The footballer Ronaldo surprises everyone by leaving to play in Germany during a winning run.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the D in RONALDO for L to get RONALLO, then rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on a roll is an idiom for enjoying a continued run of good fortune.

clue.text: With flattery, talk round Eastern European living in desperation

indicators.note: the letters are thrown into a frantic jumble

parts.note: E for Eastern and E for European, both standard abbreviations

explanation.surface: Someone flatters an Eastern European who lives in hopeless circumstances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desperation' looks like part of the scene, but 'in desperation' is the signal to jumble the letters E, E and LIVING.
explanation.definitionFit: To inveigle is to persuade someone by cajoling or coaxing, often deceitfully.

clue.text: Plays with old money children dropped

indicators.note: the children are let fall from the old money

parts.note: drachmas were the Greek currency before the euro

explanation.surface: Games played with former coins, and the children let them fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plays' looks like a verb but is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Dramas are stage plays or theatrical works.

clue.text: Diamonds I repeatedly show a Spaniard

parts.note: D is the card abbreviation for diamonds
I, then I again in Latin, which is ego

explanation.surface: A card player keeps flashing diamonds to a Spanish opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I repeatedly' gives I and then EGO, the Latin for I.
explanation.definitionFit: Diego is a common Spanish male first name, so a Spaniard could have it.

clue.text: Before leaving north, live where the best players are

indicators.note: the north letter departs from the word

parts.note: ante is Latin for before, as in antenatal
am is a form of be, meaning to exist or live

explanation.surface: Before heading north, a sports fan lives near the top team's ground.
explanation.walkthrough: ANTE without N is ATE; AM is from 'I am', to exist.
explanation.definitionFit: The first-choice squad is made up of the most skilled performers in a team.

clue.text: Bird told me to go halves, taking back note

indicators.note: the halved words take on the reversed note at the end
each of the three words is cut to its front half
the letters of the note are read in reverse

parts.note: ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A bird told someone to split a bill, taking back a banknote.
explanation.walkthrough: Halving TOLD, ME and TO gives TO, M and T; TI reversed is IT.
explanation.definitionFit: The tomtit is a small songbird, an informal name for the blue tit or similar.

clue.text: That's frightening about fan's collapse

indicators.note: turned about, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: eek is an exclamation of fright
a lover of something is a fan of it

explanation.surface: Someone startled when a supporter's stand gives way.
explanation.walkthrough: EEK reversed is KEE.
explanation.definitionFit: To keel over is to topple or faint suddenly, which is a way to collapse.

clue.text: Almost a disaster — point to what should prevent a shock

parts.note: N is the compass point north
earthing an appliance connects it to the ground to stop electric shocks

explanation.surface: A near-miss, pointing to a device meant to stop electrical shocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shock' sounds like surprise but is electric. Earthing is the British term for what Americans call grounding.
explanation.definitionFit: A near thing is a narrow escape, when disaster only just failed to happen.

clue.text: OK member of the bourgeoisie receives black mark

indicators.note: the black letter is taken inside

parts.note: a bourgeois is not a prole, a member of the working class
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
M stands for the mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A middle-class person gets a bad mark against their name.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'no prole' as one who is not working class; B goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying no problem is an informal way of agreeing or assuring someone that all is fine.
